preamble: A tribute on 8 to 26 16 across, who gave us the 1 across 25

clue.text: See 27
Let apple Danish pastries be distributed in great number for today

definitions.note: a number is a song; this one suits the day of the tribute

indicators.note: letters that are distributed are spread about, so the four words before are dealt out into a new order

explanation.surface: An instruction to hand out pastries generously.
explanation.walkthrough: 'be distributed' rearranges all the letters of LET APPLE DANISH PASTRIES, a nice touch since the song title is itself about handing something out.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the title of a well-known song, sung by Sting among others, fitting a day about smiling.

clue.text: Isn't it commonly where you get booze and sex?

parts.note: an inn is a pub, a place serving alcohol
IT is a crossword standby for sex appeal or sex

explanation.surface: A slangy question about where to find drink and company.
explanation.walkthrough: IT for sex (or sex appeal) is an old usage, as in 'she's got it'.
explanation.definitionFit: A British street-slang contraction of the tag question 'isn't it', so 'commonly' marks its informal register.

clue.text: Mid-September before a sailor's back from Asia, perhaps

indicators.note: mid- points to the central letter of the month's name, its fifth of nine

parts.note: the back of a ship, which a sailor would know as the stern

explanation.surface: Someone back from Asia in mid-September after a sailing trip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'before' simply orders the pieces: the middle letter E comes ahead of A and STERN.
explanation.definitionFit: Asia lies in the east, so something from there is oriental; 'perhaps' flags it as one example of the adjective.

clue.text: Engineer cannily takes women's perspective

parts.note: W is the standard abbreviation for women, as on toilet doors
an angle is a point of view or slant on something

explanation.surface: An engineer shrewdly adopting a female point of view.
explanation.definitionFit: To manipulate a result by cunning or trickery is to fix it artfully, which is what engineering something cannily amounts to.

clue.text: Event is a fine opportunity to have fun

parts.note: F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
a fair, with its rides and stalls, is an occasion for enjoyment

explanation.surface: Someone praising an event as a good chance to enjoy oneself.
explanation.definitionFit: An occasion or happening, as in 'a grand social affair', is a synonym for an event.

clue.text: Dickensian character of rag playing at close of 8

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters of rag are toyed with and set in a fresh order

parts.note: 8 down is WORLD SMILE DAY: the close of WORLD is D, a SMILE is a GRIN and DAY is abbreviated D

explanation.surface: A Dickens figure who plays the rag at the end of a festival day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'playing' rearranges RAG into GRA; then 8 down is broken up: D ending WORLD, GRIN for SMILE, D for DAY. 'at' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Gradgrind is the facts-obsessed schoolmaster in Dickens's novel Hard Times.

clue.text: Atmosphere Longfellow captures in no time, poetically

indicators.note: the two words hold the letters within them, as if taking them prisoner

explanation.surface: A poet's work quickly evokes a mood.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across the end of 'atmosphere' and the start of 'Longfellow', the American poet, apt for a poetic word.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic, literary word meaning soon or before long, hence 'poetically'.

clue.text: Damsel rowdily revelling for 24 life-enhancing hours

indicators.note: someone revelling is carousing wildly, so these two words are thrown about into a new order

explanation.surface: A young woman partying noisily for a whole, happy day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rowdily' looks like the anagram signal, but it is fodder; 'revelling' is the indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: An annual day, the first Friday of October, devoted to cheerful acts; a day lasts twenty-four hours.

clue.text: Gibbons show teeth and tongue, skipping closer

parts.note: to grin is to smile broadly, baring the teeth

indicators.note: skipping the closer means the last letter of the language word is left off

parts.note: lingo is slang for a language, or tongue

explanation.surface: Apes baring teeth and sticking out tongues, except the nearest one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gibbons' looks like apes, but it is the surname of the woodcarver.
explanation.definitionFit: Grinling Gibbons was the celebrated Dutch-born woodcarver; his first name completes his surname here.

clue.text: Crystallised forms of cocaine? Bogus setter's first to ingest line

parts.note: snow is slang for cocaine

indicators.note: to ingest is to take in, so one word swallows the other

parts.note: bogus means fake

indicators.note: first marks the opening letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: A query whether crystals are a form of cocaine, with the setter Bogus snorting a line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bogus' is also the setter's own pseudonym, which disguises its job as a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Ice crystals that fall as snow are crystallised water shapes, each a frozen six-sided form.

clue.text: Story about extremely truculent rabbit

indicators.note: about means around, so the story goes round the other letters

parts.note: a tale is a story

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A story concerning a very aggressive rabbit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rabbit' is not the animal: in British slang to rabbit (on) is to chatter.
explanation.definitionFit: To rabbit is British slang for chattering idly, and to gossip or prattle is a synonym.

clue.text: Hiding case of luxury gin? Silly moo!

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outer shell, the first and last letters
silly suggests the letters are muddled into a new order

parts.note: to low is to moo, as cattle do

explanation.surface: A dig at someone for posh gin, ending with an insult.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silly moo' looks like the British insult, but 'Silly' rearranges GIN and 'moo' is LOW.
explanation.definitionFit: To lie low is to stay out of sight, keeping concealed, so in the -ing form it means hiding.

clue.text: See 1 down
Park's first wild arboreal mammal

indicators.note: first takes the opening letter of the word before it
wild suggests the letters run loose into a new order

explanation.surface: A park's leading tree-dwelling creature.
explanation.definitionFit: The great white Arctic bear is a large carnivorous mammal; the definition is a broad category.

clue.text: See 9
Regularly fall ill after bachelor party

indicators.note: after places the letters picked from the phrase following the bachelor's letter

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for bachelor, as in BA

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter

explanation.surface: Someone getting sick repeatedly after a stag do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' picks the 2nd, 4th and 6th letters of FALL ILL, giving ALL.
explanation.definitionFit: A ball is a formal dancing party, the kind with gowns and an orchestra.

clue.text: Maintain Anabaptist principles, with a big 9?

definitions.meaning: split as two words, to be one of the Amish sect, Anabaptist Christians
9 across is GRIN, so this means wearing a broad smile

explanation.surface: A question whether keeping to strict Anabaptist ways goes with a big grin.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as BE AMISH it is a phrase about the Amish, Anabaptists known for plain living; as one word, a Lewis Carroll coinage.
explanation.definitionFit: Beaming with happiness and optimism; the word comes from Lewis Carroll's Jabberwocky.

clue.text: Current state of two ponies? Ruth blows top about one

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the money goes round the letter for one

parts.note: a pony is slang for 25 pounds, so two make fifty quid, written L for fifty plus QUID
I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: losing the top means the first letter of the synonym is dropped

parts.note: ruth is an old word for pity or compassion

explanation.surface: A puzzle about the state of two ponies, and someone named Ruth losing her temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruth' looks like a name, but it is the old word for compassion. A pony is British betting slang for £25.
explanation.definitionFit: Liquidity is the condition of being fluid, and a current is a flow, so this is a punning gloss.

clue.text: Cult celeb wanting outsiders to support British music-maker

indicators.note: in a down entry, a part that supports another sits beneath it

parts.note: UK, the United Kingdom, stands for British

indicators.note: lacking outsiders means the first and last letters of each word are lost

explanation.surface: A cult celebrity with no fans backing a British musician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wanting outsiders' strips CULT to UL and CELEB to ELE; 'to support' puts them under UK.
explanation.definitionFit: A small four-stringed guitar-like instrument is something that makes music.

clue.text: Cut the crap! Rearrange that number for piano

indicators.note: rearrange tells you to reorder the letters of the clue's opening words
number for piano means one letter is put in place of the other

parts.note: P is the musical abbreviation for piano, meaning softly

explanation.surface: An exasperated 'stop the nonsense', then an order to rearrange a piece for piano.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' swaps CRAP's P for N, giving CRAN; 'Rearrange' then shuffles THE CRAN. 'Cut' looks like part of the exclamation but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A tranche is a portion or slice of something, as in a tranche of funding.

clue.text: See 1
SAS perhaps on brink of triumph and verge of shock

indicators.note: on places the second part straight after the first
a brink is an edge, here the final letter of the word

parts.note: SAS is Scandinavian Airlines, an example of an airline

explanation.surface: The SAS special forces on the edge of victory, and a soldier near breakdown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'SAS' suggests the British special forces, but it is the Scandinavian carrier. 'shock' is a shock of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: The edge where hair begins on the forehead is the border of a mop of hair.

clue.text: You heard Pharrell's number one hit, Happy

indicators.note: heard tells you that the word you is spoken, giving a single letter with the same sound

parts.note: the word you is said aloud, and it sounds like the letter U

indicators.note: number one means the leading letter of the name

parts.note: to beat is to hit

explanation.surface: Pharrell Williams's chart-topping song Happy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Happy' looks like the song's title, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An upbeat mood is cheerful and optimistic, which is being happy.

clue.text: Discontented fairy keels over in pub, leaving the rest standing

indicators.note: in places the turned letters within the pub word

parts.note: a bar is a pub

indicators.note: keels over means turning upside down, so in a down entry the letters run backwards
removing a word's contents leaves just its outer letters

explanation.surface: An unhappy fairy collapsing in a pub, outlasting everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discontented' keeps only the outer letters of the fairy word, and 'keels over' fits a down entry, where the pair is turned upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: To win by far is to beat others by a wide margin, leaving them standing still.

clue.text: Graduate's recent entertaining time amid old tribesmen

definitions.note: the 's stands for is, with graduate the noun

indicators.note: entertaining means holding inside, so the recent word hosts the rest

parts.note: late can mean recent, as in the late news

indicators.note: amid means in the middle of, so the time letter goes among the tribe

parts.note: the Iceni were an ancient British tribe led by Boudicca

explanation.surface: A recent graduate's party, oddly set among ancient tribesmen.
explanation.walkthrough: The Iceni were the tribe of Boudicca in East Anglia.
explanation.definitionFit: A holder of a university licence or degree, such as a licentiate of a college, is a graduate.

clue.text: Confront female, one outranking king

parts.note: in many card games the ace ranks above the king

explanation.surface: Challenging a woman who outranks the monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: To face up to someone is to meet them head-on and confront them.

clue.text: Rabbit, one with long ears eating very last bit of celery

indicators.note: eating means taking in, so the long-eared animal holds the letter

parts.note: a hare is noted for its long ears

indicators.note: the last bit of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: A long-eared rabbit munching celery.
explanation.walkthrough: Harvey is the invisible six-foot rabbit of the play and James Stewart film; here also Harvey Ball, creator of the smiley.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of the stage play and film Harvey is a giant invisible rabbit, a pooka.

clue.text: Agent offering Hobson's choice of guide on vacation, with a 9

parts.words: Hobson's choice of guide on vacation
parts.note: guide emptied leaves GE; Hobson's choice offers no real choice, so GE OR GE
9 across is a grin, so with one is smiling

explanation.surface: An agent forced to accept an empty guide, grinning.
explanation.walkthrough: Hobson's choice, from a Cambridge stable owner, is 'this one or none': here the same pair of letters either side of OR.
explanation.definitionFit: John le Carré's spymaster in Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy is a fictional British intelligence agent.
